reading.body:
Self-hosting a model shifts the compute burden entirely onto the operator's own hardware, which means the grid constraint moves from a cloud provider's data center to wherever the organization runs its inference stack.

The six tools here span the full self-hosted pipeline: model discovery and distribution via Hugging Face Transformers, framework-level training and serving via PyTorch and TensorFlow, high-throughput inference via vLLM, and lightweight edge deployment via llama.cpp and Ollama. Each step in that chain has its own power and hardware profile. A framework checkpoint on a researcher's workstation draws trivially. The same model served at production throughput through vLLM on owned infrastructure draws as much as any cloud instance, and the operator, not a cloud vendor, is now responsible for provisioning the power and cooling.

The notes attached to these tools flag supply-chain verification, model card governance, serialization risks, and provenance tracking as recurring concerns. Those are software and policy issues, not power issues, and the data does not connect them to compute or grid load in any direct way. What the data does not cover is the hardware each tool targets, the scale at which any of them are typically deployed, or the energy characteristics of the workloads they run. A reader cannot derive from this list whether self-hosting, in aggregate, concentrates or disperses grid demand relative to centralized cloud inference.
